title: Thanksgiving Storms Leave Hundreds of Thousands in the Dark Across the U.S.
excerpt: Power outages, flight chaos and flooded streets linger a day after Thanksgiving storms battered both coasts.
body:
## East Coast Chaos
The Thanksgiving holiday turned stormy for millions of Americans as a powerful system slammed the eastern seaboard with high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania emerged as the hardest‑hit state, topping Poweroutage.us’s list of power cuts on Friday. By late afternoon more than 360,000 households were still without electricity, a figure that fell to about 260,000 by evening. The outage peak on Thursday night neared a million homes across Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey. In New York City, nearly two inches of rain drenched Central Park, setting a record for the wettest Thanksgiving at that spot. Bridges closed in Maryland, Delaware’s boardwalks were swamped, and tidal surges soaked runways at Reagan National Airport.

## Travel Turmoil
Air travel took a hit as the storms rolled through. Flightaware.com reported over 3,400 U.S. flights delayed and nearly 670 cancelled on Friday, adding to the 2,500+ delays and 450+ cancellations on Thanksgiving itself. Passengers endured long waits, with one traveler stuck at LaGuardia for 13 hours en route to Chicago. West Coast commuters faced their own challenges: high tides exceeding eight feet in San Diego and Los Angeles prompted beach closures, and Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner canceled several runs due to washout conditions.

## Looking Ahead
President Donald Trump signaled a willingness to release emergency funds as states declared emergencies and officials urged water‑use restrictions. The storm is expected to drift into Nova Scotia and Newfoundland on Saturday, offering a drier weekend for the northeastern U.S. but meteorologists warn another low‑pressure system could bring more rain and wind on Monday, potentially sparking further disruptions.

The Thanksgiving storms have left a lasting imprint—power still flickering in hundreds of thousands of homes, roads and bridges submerged, and the iconic Macy’s parade postponed for the first time in a century.
